raw_response:
Thirty years on this land, and every season I start the same way — I think about what I did last year, what my neighbor Old Wang did, and what I can afford this time around.

My 6 mu is split two ways. Four mu goes in the wheat-maize rotation — wheat in October, maize after the wheat harvest in June. That rotation is what my father did, what everyone around here does. The other 2 mu is stevia. I started doing stevia eight years ago after I saw Old Wang sell his leaves and make more money per mu than from grain. It is a cash crop. It does not feed us directly but it pays for the fertilizer.

**Wheat (4 mu, starting this October):**
I plant Kenong 199 — that variety has been doing well around Quzhou. A lot of my neighbors switched to it a few years back and I followed. Before planting I rotary till the field after the maize is harvested. I put down compound fertilizer and diammonium phosphate as base, then top up with urea at jointing. For my 4 mu I use about 5 bags of compound fertilizer plus 1 bag urea at base, then another bag of urea when the plants are knee-high. That comes out to roughly 13 kg nitrogen per mu. I irrigate three times — once before it gets cold in November to help roots settle, once at jointing in March, once at heading in April. I spray twice, once in early spring for rust, once around heading for aphids if I see them.

**Maize (4 mu, starting June after wheat harvest):**
Right after I cut the wheat I seed maize with no-till — no time to plough because the window is tight. I use Zhengdan 958. Everyone around here uses it. I apply compound fertilizer at planting, then chase with urea when the plants are about knee-high. Maize drinks a lot of nitrogen. In a dry year I irrigate twice — once around the big bell stage, once at silking. If we get good rain I might skip one. I spray once or twice for corn borer.

**Stevia (2 mu, spring through autumn):**
I plant stevia from root cuttings in late April. It needs water more than grain does. I irrigate four times through the growing season. I get three cuttings — one in July, one in August, one in October before frost. The leaf buyers from the processing plant come to the village. I apply less nitrogen than for grain but more potassium — the buyers told me potassium is good for the sweetness, and I listened because it affects my price. I rotary till before planting each spring to break up the roots from last year.
